title: Hayabusa2 Quits 1998 KY26 Mission As Avi Loeb Claims It Is Something Else; Know JAXA's Next Target
excerpt: Harvard astrophysicist Abvi Loeb had earlier stated that 1998 KY26 is far from a dark comet like the first interstellar interloper Oumuamua. Could it be the lost Soviet probe Phobos 1 that went dark in 1988? JAXA’s latest mission rejig has raised a few eyebrows for sure.
content:
JAXA has dropped its plan to send the Hayabusa2 probe to asteroid 1998 KY26, even as Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb says the timing is no accident. Per the latest report, the Japanese space agency told the Cabinet Office’s Space Policy Committee on Monday, November 16, that the spacecraft will go elsewhere. Loeb has argued that 1998 KY26, which he dubbed a dark comet like the Oumuamua, may be Phobos 1, the Soviet probe lost in 1988.

By Loeb\s own account, he made that case on Fox News a few hours after NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman told Fox & Friends there was no evidence the object was anything other than an asteroid. His claim rests on two papers co-authored with Adam Hibbard and Adam Kroll, which he in his latest tweet states met heavy pushback from journal editors, referees and social media users.

Loeb’s Theory On 1998 KY26

Loeb wrote on X that the engine trouble had been known for more than three months. Given that, he put the chance of JAXA deciding within a day of his TV appearances at under 1%. He says this points to a correlation with his appearances. He had earlier told his co-authors that the probe’s July 2031 arrival would force critics to concede, and he compared the episode to the Galileo affair. Is Loeb overreaching here with his arguments?

JAXA has cancelled its planned intercept with the “dark comet” 1998 KY26 just one day after I argued that the object may not be a comet at all, but something artificial. pic.twitter.com/JdSH0TQBzG

— Professor Avi Loeb (@ProfAviLoeb) November 16, 2026

Hayabusa2 Busted?

Per the latest updates, a fourth of Hayabusa2’s main ion engines malfunctioned in mid-August 2026. The spacecraft moved to a mode that uses the working parts of two faulty engines, which cost it thrust. Reaching 1998 KY26 in 2031 required a gravity assist near Earth, and the engines had far exceeded their design life. So?

New Target?

Hayabusa2 will fly past asteroid 2015 BM510 instead. The object is 17 to 74 meters across, and JAXA plans the flyby for 2028 to observe its surface in detail.

JAXA has decided to abandon its plan to reach asteroid 1998 KY26 due to ion drive engine troubles.

The new destination is the asteroid "2015 BM510," which is 17 to 74 meters in size. In 2028, they will perform a flyby to observe its surface in detail.
